```{r}
#| include: false
source("_helper.R")
```

A bar chart with 70 bars needs 70 labels, and on a page of ordinary width
they don't fit underneath. Bend the bars around a circle and each label gets
the space at the end of its own bar. A straight bar chart is easier to compare
precisely, but sorted by height, the circle still shows the shape of the data:
a spiral from the wettest city down to the driest.

The data is `precip`, which ships with R: average annual precipitation for 70
cities in the United States and Puerto Rico, from the *Statistical Abstract of
the United States* (1975). Two of the cities are called Portland. `precip` lists
them in state order, so the first is Maine's and the second Oregon's.

```{r}
city <- names(precip)
city[city == "Portland"] <- c("Portland, ME", "Portland, OR")
pr <- data.frame(city = city, cm = as.numeric(precip) * 2.54)
pr <- pr[order(-pr$cm), ]
pr$city <- factor(pr$city, levels = pr$city)
```

## Labels along the angle

`coord_radial()` bends the x axis into the angle and the y axis into the
radius. The labels need one more step, the same one a ggplot2 circular bar
chart takes: work out each bar's angle and turn its text to match. With 70 bars
starting at twelve o'clock and running clockwise, bar *i* sits at
90° − 360° × (*i* − ½) / 70. On the left half of the circle that angle would
put the text upside down, so those labels turn another 180° and are anchored at
their right end (`hjust = 1`) instead of their left. The number goes on the
inner side, so it always sits next to the bar.

```{r}
n <- nrow(pr)
ang <- 90 - 360 * (seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n
pr$right <- ang > -90
pr$angle <- ifelse(pr$right, ang, ang + 180)
pr$label <- ifelse(pr$right,
                   paste0(pr$city, "  ", round(pr$cm)),
                   paste0(round(pr$cm), "  ", pr$city))
pr$label_at <- pr$cm + 4
```

## What is drawn

- `mark_bar()` with an explicit `y` draws one bar per city at its height, filled
  on a continuous scale from sand to deep teal.
- Two `mark_text()` layers draw the labels, one for each half of the circle,
  each with its `angle` mapped and its own `hjust`.
- The y limits start below zero at −45. That opens the hole in the middle: the
  radius is the y scale, so the bars start some way out from the centre, where
  the circle is wide enough to hold them.
- `theme_minimal()` with the axis text turned off leaves only the circular
  gridlines, which show behind the shorter bars.

```{r}
p <- vplot(pr, width = 7.5, height = 8) |>
  mark_bar(x = city, y = cm, fill = cm) |>
  mark_text(data = pr[pr$right, ], x = city, y = label_at, label = label,
            angle = angle, hjust = 0, size = 7) |>
  mark_text(data = pr[!pr$right, ], x = city, y = label_at, label = label,
            angle = angle, hjust = 1, size = 7) |>
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#e8d9b5", "#9fb3a1", "#3f6e78", "#1f3b4d")) |>
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-45, 185), breaks = c(50, 100, 150)) |>
  coord_radial() |>
  labs(
    title = "How wet is the year?",
    subtitle = "Average annual precipitation in 70 US cities, in centimetres, wettest first",
    caption = "Data: datasets::precip (Statistical Abstract of the United States, 1975)"
  ) |>
  theme_minimal() |>
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Circular bar chart of annual precipitation in 70 US cities, sorted from Mobile (170 cm) at twelve o'clock clockwise down to Phoenix (18 cm), each bar labelled with its city and value along its angle"
vg(p, "circular-bars", dpi = 130)
```

Mobile, Alabama tops the list at 170 cm a year, followed by Miami, San Juan
and New Orleans: the Gulf and the Caribbean. The bottom of the spiral is the
desert Southwest and the interior West: Phoenix gets 18 cm, Reno and El Paso
about 20. Most of the East sits in a narrow band around a metre, which is where
the spiral flattens out.

For bars in polar space without the labels, see the
[coxcomb](coxcomb.qmd); for text that follows a curve rather than a straight
angle, see [labels that follow the curve](text-path.qmd).
